bill.title: the GENIUS Act
bill.description: S.1582 creates federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital coins an issuer must redeem for a fixed dollar value. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue them, and each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets that issuers may not lend out.
bill.main_effect_html: The bill sets national rules for stablecoin issuers: companies that promise to redeem digital money for a fixed sum. The rules cover financial backing, repayment and controls on unlawful payments. “This bill establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins (digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value).” [1]

values.main_effect_html: S.1582 would create national licensing and safeguards for payment stablecoins, “digital assets which an issuer must redeem for a fixed value” [1]. On July 17, 2025, they were regulated “as money transmitters, primarily at the state level” [2]. The bill would require permitted issuers to back their tokens with reserves “on an at least 1 to 1 basis” [3]. If an issuer fails, holders would get priority on those reserves: “over the claims of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and any other holder of claims against the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [3].

values.reference: Read this value as held by an average American: ordinary personal health and safety risks in U.S. circumstances, without assuming a specially exposed person.
values.main_effect_html: S.1582 would strengthen controls on payment stablecoins, digital payment tokens “redeemable at a predetermined fixed amount (e.g., $1).” [1] It builds on existing law: “reporting requirements for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) apply equally to the transmission of crypto assets.” [2] Section 4 makes the ability and duty to obey federal blocking orders a condition of issuing tokens: “only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [3] These orders can require issuers to “seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person” [3]. Section 8 also conditions foreign stablecoins’ availability through U.S. service providers on the issuer’s ability to obey and actual compliance. Treasury can enforce this through a notice “prohibiting digital asset service providers from facilitating secondary trading of payment stablecoins issued by the foreign payment stablecoin issuer in the United States.” [3]

values.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
values.main_effect_html: S.1582 adds national safeguards for payment stablecoins—digital tokens redeemable for a fixed amount of money. Approved issuers must hold “at least one dollar of permitted reserves for every one dollar of stablecoins issued.” [1] These are assets set aside to repay users. Before the bill, state oversight generally imposed “more limited requirements than the bills propose.” [2]

claims.title: The bill would increase stablecoin use overall
claims.statement: Compared with the law in force on July 17, 2025, S.1582's national rules and clearer legal permission would tend to increase the issuance or use of payment stablecoins at least somewhat. This claim does not say how much, how fast, or who the new users would be.
claims.background_html:
A payment stablecoin is a digital token. A company called the issuer promises to exchange it for a fixed amount of money, such as $1. This exchange is called redemption. CRS says the bill “establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins” [TR 15].

All the arguments compare S.1582 with the law in force on July 17, 2025. Existing rules were “mainly a diverse set of state money transmitter licensing requirements” [TR 14].
claims.support_html:
The administration says the bill “removes regulatory uncertainty that has hindered innovation and competitiveness in the digital assets sector.” [UNC 35] The White House describes the aim as attracting digital-asset activity by “providing clear rules and promoting responsible innovation in the stablecoin market” [TR 16].

The New Yorker reports that major banks “largely stayed away from them, put off by regulatory uncertainty and crypto’s association with illicit transactions.” [UNC 36]

The bill opens a national route: “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [TR 1] Section 16 says: “Entities regulated by the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators are authorized to engage in the payment stablecoin activities and investments contemplated by this Act” [UNN 2]. CRS says: “The GENIUS Act codified permission for banks to issue their own stablecoins and perform other activities, thereby strengthening certain linkages between industries.” [SES 28]

Two analyses predict growth. AEI writes: “The passage of either bills will likely accelerate the integration of private stablecoins into the retail banking environment.” [SES 29] CFR writes: “The passage of the GENIUS Act is expected to lead to rapid growth in the circulation of bank-issued dollar stablecoins.” [SES 22] These are forecasts. CFR's sentence is about bank-issued coins.
claims.objection_html:
No response in the bank directly denies that the bill would add some use. That absence does not prove the claim.

The notes limit the claim. Some bank permission existed before the bill. Brookings warns against overstating volumes. These notes limit size and timing. No minimum size is needed for this claim.
claims.notes_html:
S1582_UNN-3

Evidence note: OCC said in January 2021 that national banks and federal savings associations may use stablecoins for payment activities, and in March 2025 rescinded its supervisory nonobjection requirement. Innovo's July 2025 article says it had 'already operationalized' stablecoin settlement. Sources: [UNN 16], [UNN 17], [UNN 14].

S1582_SES-4

Evidence note: OCC confirmed in March 2025 that certain stablecoin activities are permissible and rescinded its nonobjection requirement. The bill also has a route for foreign issuers. Sources: [SES 21], [SES 4].

S1582_UNC-16b

Evidence note: Brookings cautions against overstating stablecoin volumes: without interest, holders have incentives to minimize their holdings, and faster payments let a given volume of stablecoins support more payments. The same paper describes these coins as a substitute for cash or bank transaction accounts. CRS says depositors who shift lose federal insurance, a risk exposure some consumers may not be aware of. Sources: [UNC 37], [UNC 30].

claims.title: The bill would lead to more Bitcoin mining
claims.statement: By expanding and legitimizing stablecoins and crypto, S.1582 would tend to lead to more Bitcoin mining than would happen without it. This claim does not say how much more.
claims.background_html: Bitcoin is a different crypto asset from a stablecoin. Its price moves, and it “can only be created through mining” [UNN 25]. Mining is computer work that earns new coins and fees. It uses a lot of electricity. A stablecoin needs no mining, so this claim runs through Bitcoin trading and wider acceptance of crypto.
claims.support_html:
Reward route. Brookings reported: “Stablecoins currently are used mainly for trading crypto assets” [UNN 21]. A study found that “stablecoins increase the trading volume of Bitcoin.” [UNN 22] The White House science office explains: “As a crypto-asset becomes more valuable, the mining rewards also become more valuable. This attracts more miners and computing resources to solve the cryptographic math problem.” [UNN 23]

Acceptance route. Earthjustice clean-energy attorney Mandy DeRoche says: “The more that crypto currency generally is legitimized and used, the more crypto mining there will be” [UNN 24].

The arguments add: running stablecoins on low-energy networks leaves their role in Bitcoin trading in place, and mining rewards still attract computing power as Bitcoin's value grows.
claims.objection_html:
This response challenges the whole bill-to-mining step, so it applies to all seven mining arguments.

Trading volume is not price. Volume measures how much changes hands, not how much the price rises. A 2018 study found: “Tether issuances do not impact subsequent Bitcoin returns, however, they do impact traded volumes.” [UNN 27] Returns means price gains or losses. A 2020 study of Tether flows reports: “We find no significant effect on the prices of Bitcoin and Ethereum” [UNN 28], while adding that its results “do not discount the possibility that price manipulation can occur” [UNN 28]. The coal-plant study tests a price change: “We exploit daily variation in Bitcoin price as a natural experiment for an 86 megawatt coal-fired power plant with on-site cryptomining.” [UNN 26]

Permission is not buying. Section 16 says: “Entities regulated by the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators are authorized to engage in the payment stablecoin activities and investments contemplated by this Act” [UNN 2]. That permission does not itself establish more Bitcoin buying. Stablecoins also serve sellers: the 2020 study describes investors “liquidating their Bitcoin holdings” [UNN 28] into Tether during a price crash.

Exchange trades may pay miners nothing. Miners collect “fees associated with transactions within the block.” [UNN 23] But “centralized crypto-asset trading platforms typically use off-chain transactions” [UNN 23], meaning trades recorded inside the platform and not in Bitcoin's shared record.

The forecast. The response says DeRoche's broad forecast does not resolve this evidence or show that the bill would raise miner fees.

What remains unanswered: the response shows a missing link. It does not show that the bill would add no mining. The price-null studies have limits, stated in the note below.
claims.notes_html:
S1582_UNN-5

Evidence note: The cited price-null studies analyze Tether issuance or flows in samples ending by 2020 and do not study legal recognition. The price-emissions study covers one 86 MW Pennsylvania coal plant, and the OSTP report dates from 2022. Sources: [UNN 28], [UNN 27], [UNN 26].

prerequisite_paths.reason: Reward route: more stablecoin use leads to more Bitcoin trading, then higher Bitcoin value, then higher mining rewards. This route needs added stablecoin use.

Legitimation route: DeRoche's forecast links wider acceptance of crypto generally to more mining. It does not pass through a measured rise in payment-stablecoin use, so it stays open if C01 is No, but its only support is that forecast, and the forecast joins 'legitimized' to 'used'.

claims.title: Permitted issuers must hold full backing
claims.statement: S.1582 requires each permitted issuer to keep identifiable reserves worth at least one dollar for each dollar of coins outstanding, held in a listed set of assets. This claim does not say the reserves will always be available as cash during stress, and it does not cover coins from issuers without permission.
claims.background_html: Reserves are assets an issuer sets aside to repay people who hold its coins. Permitted issuers are companies approved under the bill. The rule covers these issuers. Tether is “licensed in El Salvador” [TR 2], so the rules for approved issuers reach it only if it becomes one.
claims.support_html:
Section 4 says a permitted issuer shall “maintain identifiable reserves backing the outstanding payment stablecoins of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer on an at least 1 to 1 basis” [UNC 3].

CRS: “Issuers would be required to hold at least one dollar of permitted reserves for every one dollar of stablecoins issued.” [UNN 12] CRS also says: “The bill would limit permitted reserves to coins and currency, deposits held at insured banks and credit unions, short-dated Treasury bills” [UNC 4].

CRS summary: “Permitted issuers must maintain reserves backing the stablecoin on a one-to-one basis using U.S. currency or other similarly liquid assets, as specified.” [SES 1]
claims.objection_html:
No response denies the duty. Responses and notes concern what the duty achieves:

Brookings says “the permissible reserve assets include uninsured deposits in banks and shares of credit unions” [SES 12] and “uninsured deposits are risky and illiquid” [SES 12]. The source says this raises the possibility of unstable value and runs, unless capital, liquidity and risk management standards reduce those risks. Some of those standards are still to be written.

A response to SES_support_02 says the bill also allows “money received under repurchase agreements, with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer acting as a seller of securities” [SES 4]. That response is kept with that argument.

What remains unanswered: the legal duty itself.
claims.notes_html:
S1582_UNC-1

Evidence note: Before the vote, Circle described full, liquid and unencumbered reserves and monthly third-party assurance. New York's guidance required full backing, timely par redemption and public CPA reports for stablecoins under its supervision, and New York licensing rules required cyber programs and background reports. New York rules applied only to New York-supervised issuers. Sources: [UNC 9], [UNC 10], [UNC 11].

S1582_TR-2

Evidence note: Circle reported in 2022 that USDC reserves were held in segregated accounts for holders, with third-party monthly attestations. The cited church and fundraiser reports do not identify custody arrangements or how long gifts stay in coins. Sources: [TR 9], [TR 7], [TR 8].

claims.title: Holders come first on required reserves if an issuer fails
claims.statement: In an insolvency of a permitted issuer, people holding its coins have priority, shared in proportion to their claims, over the issuer and other claim holders with respect to required reserves. This claim does not say when holders are paid or that reserves will be enough.
claims.background_html: When a company fails, a court process decides who gets paid first. A creditor is someone the company owes money. Ratable means shared in proportion to what each person is owed.
claims.support_html: Section 11 says “the claim of a person holding payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer shall have priority, on a ratable basis with the claims of other persons holding such payment stablecoins” [UNC 3], “over the claims of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and any other holder of claims against the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, with respect to required payment stablecoin reserves” [UNN 2].
claims.objection_html:
Treasury backing a lender can take first. Section 4 permits using Treasury reserves as collateral for borrowing to meet redemptions: “creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins” [UNC 3]. Brookings explains these secured loans, called repurchase agreements or repo: in bankruptcy, “the repo lender could seize the Treasury collateral if the stablecoin issuer could not return the cash.” [UNC 13] Then “assets in segregated accounts would fall short of what is needed for 1:1 redemption.” [UNC 13] A right to share those assets does not restore the seized collateral.

What remains unanswered: protection against other business debts. The response challenges a full proportionate share only where backing has been pledged this way. For timing, see C08.
claims.notes_html: No evidence note in the bank is attached to this proposition. See the notes on each member argument.

claims.title: Firms holding stablecoin assets must keep them for customers
claims.statement: Firms covered by Section 10 must treat stablecoin assets they hold for customers as customer property, take appropriate steps to protect it from their own creditors, and generally keep it separate from their own assets. Exceptions include omnibus accounts and reserve cash held as a bank deposit.
claims.background_html: Some firms hold stablecoin assets for others. Section 10 covers firms safeguarding stablecoin reserves, coins used as collateral, or private keys (secret codes that control coins) used to issue coins. Segregated means kept separate, not mixed with the firm's own money. Here, “the person” means the firm holding the assets.
claims.support_html:
A covered firm must treat customer property “as belonging to such customer and not as the property of such person” [UNC 3].

It must “take such steps as are appropriate to protect the payment stablecoins, private keys, cash, and other property of a customer from the claims of creditors of the person.” [SES 4]

The general rule is that the property “shall be segregated from and not be commingled with the assets of the person.” [SES 4]
claims.objection_html:
A cash exception. Bank deposits held as reserves “shall not be subject to any requirement relating to the separation of such cash from the property of the applicable depository institution” [SES 4]. So the general separation rule does not shield that cash from the bank's own failure.

The section also allows omnibus accounts, which hold assets of more than one issuer or customer together at certain institutions.

What remains unanswered: the duty for other property held by covered firms.

claims.title: A failed issuer's holders can face a pause before repayment
claims.statement: In a permitted issuer's bankruptcy, the automatic stay can pause holders' redemptions until a court acts. The bill gives a faster route, but its 14-day target is a best-efforts target that runs from a hearing. This claim concerns the pause itself; it does not say the pause is new compared with prior law.
claims.background_html: The automatic stay is a bankruptcy rule. It pauses actions to collect money from a failed company until a court allows them. CRS describes this as a power to “allow a bankruptcy court to issue automatic stays on stablecoin redemptions.” [SEP 1] During a pause, a holder may have a legal claim but no spendable money.
claims.support_html:
Lawyers write: “Section 11(c) of the proposed Act applies the automatic stay to actions against the reserves.” [UNC 38]

The same lawyers say the bill “provides an accelerated procedure for stablecoin holders to obtain relief from the automatic stay” [UNC 38]. But “the court shall use best efforts to enter a final order to begin distributions under this paragraph not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [UNC 3] This is a best-efforts target. It runs from a hearing and concerns beginning payouts, not finishing them.

CRS summary: “The bill would grant stablecoin holders priority over all other claims against the issuer in bankruptcy and would allow a bankruptcy court to issue automatic stays on stablecoin redemptions.” [SES 25]
claims.objection_html:
Is the pause new? Ordinary bankruptcy already pauses claims: the stay “prevents creditors from enforcing their claims against assets of the bankruptcy estate” [UNC 38]. The issuer's request for release comes on “the petition date or as soon as practicable thereafter” [UNC 3]. One response says the pause is not shown to be a new burden, and that the bill adds a faster release route.

What remains unanswered: the same response leaves open the point that wider use would expose more people to any pause that remains. Answer this claim by whether the pause can happen. Whether it is new does not decide this claim.
claims.notes_html:
S1582_MAIN-SEP-01

Evidence note: Waller describes limited retail use and says a significant retail impact would probably take years. Below-par resales and bankruptcy stays were possible before this bill. These facts limit scale and timing and identify the baseline; they do not by themselves refute the PRO's conditional exposure route. Sources: [SEP 25], [SEP 23], [SEP 26].

Source context for main-agent review: the same lawyers write, “It would normally follow then that the automatic stay would not apply to assets not included in the bankruptcy estate” [UNC 38], and then say Section 11(c) applies it to the reserves anyway. So the pause on reserves may not simply repeat ordinary law. The current response does not discuss this passage.

claims.title: Runs on stablecoins can pull money out of banks
claims.statement: Because reserves may be held as bank deposits, including uninsured deposits, a rush to redeem stablecoins can pull money out of banks. This claim concerns that mechanism, not its expected size. The reverse direction, from bank trouble to a stablecoin run, is background and is not needed for a Yes.
claims.background_html: A run is when many people demand their money at once. Breaking the buck means falling below the promised $1 value. Uninsured deposits are bank balances above the government insurance limit. Issuers may hold part of their reserves as bank deposits. This links them to banks.
claims.support_html:
Brookings: “Similarly, a stablecoin issuer deemed at risk of breaking the buck could lead to a rapid withdrawal of deposits at banks that otherwise were sound.” [SEP 22]

Brookings: “Stress at the bank that holds the PPSI’s uninsured deposits could trigger a stablecoin run and a stablecoin run would accelerate the deposit outflow from the already-stressed bank.” [SES 34] PPSI means a permitted issuer.

Brookings also describes both directions: “Moreover, allowing stablecoins to hold uninsured bank deposits creates direct two-way interconnections between the risk of banks and the risk of stablecoins.” [SEP 30] Only the direction from a run to banks is needed for this claim.

New York Fed researchers, studying banks serving one issuer, find: “Stablecoins directly transmit liquidity shocks to the banking system” [SEP 31]. These shocks are sudden demands for ready cash.
claims.objection_html:
None of the three arguments has a point-specific CON. That does not prove the claim.

The notes limit it. Regulators reaffirmed deposit permission before the bill. Partner banks keep larger reserves to manage this exposure. The bill directs diversification rules. Rules on capital and liquidity are still to be written.
claims.notes_html:
S1582_SEP-5

Evidence note: Federal guidance in March 2025 reaffirmed permission to hold deposits backing stablecoins in certain circumstances. The NY Fed study reports partner banks retain larger reserve balances to manage liquidity exposure. The bill directs diversification rules and lets deposit insurers limit reserve deposits on safety grounds. Sources: [SEP 32], [SEP 31], [SEP 3].

S1582_UNC-11

Evidence note: Section 4 requires capital, liquidity and diversification rules still to be written, and it conditions repo use. Brookings frames the fire-sale danger as arising without appropriate standards; CSIS says the Act imposes no hard liquidity, concentration or stress-testing requirements. Sources: [UNC 3], [UNC 13], [UNC 43].

S1582_SES-7

Evidence note: The researchers cited by the PRO say the Act substantially improves reserve quality and disclosure. Brookings says issuer capital requirements can be lower and simpler than banks' because issuers do not take deposits and lend. The BIS data cover January 2021 to March 2025, before the bill. Sources: [SES 9], [SES 5], [SES 32].

prerequisite_paths.reason: Mechanism described by Brookings and shown for one issuer's partner banks by New York Fed researchers.

claims.title: Stablecoin growth would reduce deposit funding for local lending
claims.statement: If stablecoin use grows, some money would leave deposits at lenders that rely on local deposits, in a way that leaves those lenders with less funding for loans, and issuers themselves cannot replace those loans. This claim does not say how much or name any one lender.
claims.background_html: Banks and credit unions use deposits to fund loans. If people move money into stablecoins, the question is where that money ends up. An issuer that buys Treasury bills pays the seller, and the seller may put that money back in a bank. This claim asks about lenders that rely on local deposits. Each argument adds its own group: poor and rural areas, local firms and farms, or ministry lenders.
claims.support_html:
A lending analysis warns that deposits “could flow out of insured depository institutions and into payment stablecoins.” [UNC 29] CRS says stablecoins could “reduce banks’ deposit base as the stablecoin market grows.” [SES 16]

A Federal Reserve researcher: “a sustained migration of these funds into stablecoins reduces the funding available for loan growth unless alternative liabilities are secured.” [TR 32] In plain words, a lender must replace departing deposits to keep funding new loans.

INET: “The loss of bank deposits will severely impair the ability of community and regional banks to provide much-needed loans to consumers and Main Street businesses.” [SES 36] “Nonbank stablecoin issuers cannot replace those lost loans because they must invest virtually all their assets in designated short-term financial instruments held as reserves.” [SES 36]

PPI: “Yet unlike deposits at banks, stablecoins have no community lending obligations.” [SES 37]
claims.objection_html:
The size figures are not forecasts. The rural warning rests on “a one-third decline in deposit levels” [UNC 29]. CRS describes the underlying pool as a “$6.6 trillion market” [UNC 30] identified as potentially at risk. The Treasury advisory presentation labels its scenarios “Hypothetical Design Components That Could Influence Market Behaviour” [UNC 31].

Money can return to banks. When an issuer buys Treasury bills, the Council of Economic Advisers says deposits are “unchanged—they have simply moved from one institution to another.” [UNC 32] It adds: “most stablecoin deposits end up redeposited elsewhere in the banking system and able to be lent out.” [SES 39]

It depends. “The impact on U.S. bank deposits depends on who demands stablecoins, what assets are converted for stablecoin purchase, and how stablecoin issuers manage reserves.” [SES 38] It also depends on “whether counterparties to stablecoin issuers ultimately deposit proceeds back into the banking system.” [SES 38] “Early adoption patterns suggest stablecoins may initially draw more heavily from investment products before significantly impacting core deposits held at banks.” [TR 32]

Other routes. “A bank could issue a stablecoin through a subsidiary, and keep its entire stablecoin reserve balances in demand deposits at its parent bank.” [SES 40] CRS says some uses, including foreign remittances and foreigners' savings, are “not likely to cause substitution with U.S. deposits.” [SES 16]

What remains unanswered: a total staying the same does not show that each local lender keeps its funding. The responses themselves say the question is which local banks lose usable funding.
claims.notes_html:
S1582_UNC-8

Evidence note: The PPI lending warning builds on a $6.6 trillion figure that CRS and the Treasury advisory presentation describe as at risk or hypothetical. CEA's April 2026 baseline estimates that eliminating stablecoin yield would raise bank lending by $2.1 billion (0.02%), with $500 million from community banks (0.026%). Sources: [UNC 30], [UNC 31], [UNC 32].

Source context for main-agent review: in the CEA passage, “Bank A loses a deposit, Bank B gains one” [UNC 32], and “the regulatory treatment of the deposit in Bank B may be less (or more) favorable” [UNC 32]. So the redeposit point concerns total deposits; it leaves open which bank loses them.

claims.title: The ban on issuer interest removes one pull on bank deposits
claims.statement: S.1582 bars issuers from paying holders interest or yield solely for holding or using a coin, and this removes one incentive that could otherwise draw money away from bank deposits that support lending. The claim concerns payments by issuers; it does not say all rewards are barred.
claims.background_html: Interest or yield is money paid for holding funds. Banks can use deposits to make loans. If issuers could pay interest, some people might move money from bank accounts into coins. This claim is about issuers. Exchanges and other firms are a separate matter.
claims.support_html:
The bill says: “No permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield” [UNC 3].

Brookings says of such interest: “It also could draw funds away from bank deposits that underpin lending to households and businesses and are a key transmission channel for monetary policy.” [UNC 5] A transmission channel is a route by which central-bank decisions reach the economy.
claims.objection_html:
Neither argument has a point-specific CON. That does not prove the claim. Two notes limit it, without being automatic rebuttals:

Size. CEA's baseline estimate of the effect on lending is small. No minimum size is needed here.

Other rewards. CRS says “GENIUS does not explicitly prevent exchanges from paying rewards on stablecoins held on their exchange” [UNC 30], and AAF says issuers can effectively get around the ban through exchanges or third parties. So the ban removes one incentive, not all of them.

S1582_UNC-16

Evidence note: CRS reports that much retail stablecoin use occurs through exchanges, that GENIUS does not explicitly prevent exchanges from paying rewards on coins they hold, that many do, and that Circle pays part of its reserve interest to Coinbase. CRS also says the issuer is prohibited from paying interest in a direct issuer-to-customer model, that the restriction would presumably apply to self-custody, and that 'holder' is undefined. Coinbase attributes part of its USDC balance growth to its rewards program. AAF says issuers can effectively circumvent the ban through exchanges or third parties. claims.title: Legal power over known payments: permitted issuers
claims.statement: S.1582 legally requires permitted issuers to have the ability to block, freeze and reject specific impermissible transactions, and to obey lawful federal orders that name the coins or accounts. This claim concerns legal duty only. It does not say that anyone can identify illegal payments, that orders will be issued or obeyed, or what happens afterward.
claims.background_html:
To block or freeze means to stop coins from moving. Issuers can do this because they control the software of their coins. A lawful order is a final, valid requirement under federal law from a court or authorized agency.

Keep four questions separate: (1) Is there a legal power to stop a known payment? This claim asks only that. (2) Can anyone identify the illegal payment? See C18 and C19. (3) Will the power actually be used? (4) What happens later, such as less crime? Each argument handles (3) and (4).
claims.support_html:
Section 4 requires “technical capabilities, policies, and procedures to block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” [UNN 2].

Section 4 also says: “A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue payment stablecoins only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [SES 4] Such orders require an issuer to “seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person” [SES 4]. They must be “issued or promulgated under Federal law” [UNN 2] and specify “the payment stablecoins or accounts subject to blocking with reasonable particularity” [UNN 2].

Steptoe: “However, the GENIUS Act now makes such capabilities a legal prerequisite for operation.” [UNT 8] Freezing reaches tokens “held by persons with no relationship to the issuer and regardless of whether the tokens are in a custodial or non-custodial wallet.” [UNT 8] A non-custodial wallet is one a person controls without a company holding the coins.
claims.objection_html:
No response denies this legal duty. Several responses say directly that they leave the blocking of identified funds open, and then target identification instead.

One limit comes from the definition of a lawful order: it must name the coins or accounts. So the duty works only once targets are identified. This is a question for C18 and C19.

The notes show that some issuers already froze funds voluntarily. They limit what the bill adds compared with prior practice, but a legal duty still differs from a voluntary choice.
claims.notes_html:
S1582_UNN-1

Evidence note: Before the vote, Tether reported voluntarily assisting with freezes in over 900 law-enforcement requests over three years, about 460 from U.S. agencies, and reported more than $2.5 billion in frozen USDT. Sources: [UNN 8].

claims.statement: S.1582 lets U.S. digital asset service providers offer a foreign issuer's coin only if that issuer can comply and does comply with lawful orders, and Treasury can bar those providers from helping trade the coins of an issuer that defies an order. The written duties are in C27. FinCEN says such reporting lets investigators “follow the money behind the illicit fentanyl supply chain, identify and prosecute the illicit actors” [SEP 4]. claims.title: Section 9 would lead to monitoring beyond issuers' own dealings
claims.statement: Section 9(d) requires FinCEN to write standards for issuers' systems to monitor blockchain transactions, and this would likely lead issuers to watch at least some transfers beyond their direct dealings. The rules are unwritten; this claim does not require a specific final rule.
claims.background_html: FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. A blockchain is a shared digital record of transfers. Primary transactions are purchases or sales with the issuer. Secondary transactions are between other people. This claim is used on both sides: some arguments want more monitoring to find crime, and one fears it exposes private ties. Answer only whether it would likely happen.
claims.support_html:
Section 9(d) requires guidance and rules on “Standards for payment stablecoin issuers' systems and practices to monitor transactions on blockchains, digital asset mixing services, tumblers, or other similar services” [SES 4]. Mixers and tumblers hide payment trails.

Steptoe: “At present, stablecoin issuers are responsible for AML compliance with respect to primary market transactions to which they are a party, but are not expected to monitor all transactions across the entirety of the blockchain.” [UNT 8] It reads the text as one that “strongly suggests that FinCEN's rules or guidance will expect PPSIs to monitor and intervene in transactions in both the primary and, to at least some degree, secondary markets.” [UNT 8]
claims.objection_html:
FinCEN's later proposal. In April 2026: “FinCEN is not proposing to require a PPSI as part of an AML/CFT program to monitor secondary market activity” [UNT 23]. “FinCEN is also not proposing to require PPSIs to file SARs on secondary market transactions” [UNT 23]. The proposal is not final and is separate from Section 9.

Section 9's rules are unwritten. They must be “based on the results of the research and risk assessments required under this section” [UNT 3], which must consider “Privacy risks associated with the information that is collected or reviewed.” [UNT 3] Guidance or rules are due within 3 years.

What remains unanswered: the outcome is open. A statutory guarantee of a specific rule is not required by this claim, but a coder should weigh Steptoe's reading against FinCEN's proposal.

Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [UNN 9].

Evidence note: Tether announced Chainalysis monitoring of secondary markets in 2024 and confirmed adoption in May 2025. Section 9 research must consider the amount and sensitivity of information and privacy risks, and FinCEN's guidance or rules are due within 3 years. The cited Cato commentary discusses earlier bill drafts. The two Supreme Court cases concern government demands for membership or donor records. Sources: [UNT 24], [UNT 25], [UNT 3], [UNT 20].

arguments.title: It strengthens tools for stopping payments for crimes that destroy nature.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 It strengthens tools for stopping payments for crimes that destroy nature.

  • Because The bill gives approved stablecoin issuers a legal duty. They must have “technical capabilities, policies, and procedures to block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” [2]. See C13. To block or freeze means to stop coins from moving.
  • Because Foreign coins sold through U.S. trading services also depend on obeying lawful orders. See C14. Treasury can bar U.S. service providers from trading a foreign issuer's coins after it defies an order.
  • Because Stablecoins provide a payment route for illicit gold. A March 2026 investigation reports: “Some of the gold originating from Guyana is reportedly sold in Venezuela in exchange for Tether, a cryptocurrency stablecoin pegged to the US dollar.” [3]
  • Because Gold mining destroys forests and pollutes soil: “Deforestation due to gold mining wipes out tropical rainforests and contaminates soil with heavy metals” [4].
  • Because Wildlife traffickers also use digital currencies. A conservation practitioners' forum reports that “criminal networks involved in IWT are increasingly leveraging cryptocurrencies for payments, laundering profits, and facilitating global operations.” [5] IWT means illegal wildlife trade.
  • Because Wildlife trafficking “threatens critical biodiversity, damages fragile ecosystems” [6].
  • Because Financial checks help stop these crimes. FinCEN, Treasury's financial-crime agency, says suspicious-payment reports and compliance with financial-crime rules “are crucial to identifying and stopping environmental crimes and related money laundering.” [6]
  • Note Existing rules already required “customer due diligence, and transaction monitoring of clients” [7]. The bill's addition is explicit freezing duties and enforceable conditions on foreign issuers' access to U.S. trading services.
  • So For environmental-crime payments covered by lawful U.S. orders, the bill strengthens the means to interrupt payments and seize proceeds. Giving authorities stronger tools against activities that destroy forests and wildlife serves [NAME]'s wish to defend nature.
arguments.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Before the vote, Tether reported voluntarily assisting with freezes in over 900 law-enforcement requests over three years, about 460 from U.S. agencies, and reported more than $2.5 billion in frozen USDT. Sources: [8].

Evidence note: The wildlife-trade source discusses cryptocurrencies generally and does not name stablecoins. The gold report's Tether statement is worded 'reportedly' and names no wallets or orders. Sources: [5], [3].

Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [9].

arguments.title: It better protects donations used to defend forests.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 It better protects donations used to defend forests.

  • Because Rainforest Foundation US (RFUS) already accepts stablecoin gifts: “RFUS accepts donations in various popular cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and USDC.” [10] USDC is a stablecoin: reporting on solar payments identifies it as “the stablecoin USDC” [11].
  • Because This route saves money for forest protection: “Crypto donations have lower transaction fees for RFUS than traditional payment methods, enabling more funds to go directly to rainforest protection and supporting Indigenous communities.” [10]
  • Because It also lets donors follow their transfers, giving them “the ability to track contributions in real time.” [10]
  • Because The bill requires full backing for approved coins. Issuers must hold at least one dollar of reserves for each dollar of coins. See C04.
  • Because If an issuer fails, coin holders come first for repayment from required reserves. See C05.
  • Because The bill also keeps required reserves outside the pool used to pay an issuer's other debts in bankruptcy. It “amends Section 541 of the Bankruptcy Code to exclude stablecoin reserves from property of the bankruptcy estate” [13].
  • Because This protection applies only while a gift remains a stablecoin. RFUS reports that it “immediately exchanges most of the crypto donations it receives for US dollars.” [10] So coverage reaches USDC gifts during processing and any share not exchanged at once.
  • So The lower fees and tracking already existed. The bill's addition is protection for gifts while held as approved stablecoins. These rules reduce the risk that issuer failure or other debts divert those gifts. Protecting this way to give preserves money for forest defense and helps [NAME] take part in defending nature.

arguments.title: It opens a clearer legal path to faster payments for renewable electricity.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 It opens a clearer legal path to faster payments for renewable electricity.

  • Because Section 16 gives firms under federal banking regulators clear permission to handle stablecoins. See C01.
  • Because Legal uncertainty held back use. Environmental-market operator Innovo describes institutional stablecoin payments as “something many were reluctant to do without legal clarity.” [14]
  • Because Innovo already uses stablecoins in its energy markets: “At Innovo, we built stablecoin settlement directly into our digital infrastructure, so all energy transactions on our platform experience a new way of settlement and finance.” [14]
  • Because These trades include credits for renewable electricity: “Whether you're trading renewable energy credits, settling transactions in energy markets, or moving carbon offsets, stablecoins offer a functioning and faster modern market than legacy systems.” [14]
  • Because Faster payment releases money tied up during trades: “When you’re not locking up funds for days at a time, you can put that money to work elsewhere, sooner.” [14]
  • Because Innovo directs this point to clean-energy participants, naming “a corporate energy buyer, a project developer, or an institution active in clean energy markets” [14].
  • Because Solar projects already use this payment method. Fortune reports: “Owners of each farm receive the stablecoin USDC for the production of Glow carbon credits” [11].
  • Because Glow's stated funding model targets projects needing help to get built: “Glow seeks out solar farms that are borderline viable and gives them just barely enough money to get them over the line for construction” [11].
  • Because Renewable electricity helps cut climate pollution. A U.S. energy-lab review finds that “total life cycle GHG emissions from renewables and nuclear energy are much lower and generally less variable than those from fossil fuels.” [15] This counts gases that warm the climate over the equipment's whole life.
  • So The bill's clear rules help institutions use faster payments in renewable-energy markets. Releasing money sooner modestly improves the finances of participants in those markets, including developers, and the solar example shows that some projects operate near the edge of viability. This inference does not specify an amount of new renewable power. Making this finance easier to use serves [NAME]'s wish to protect nature from pollution.
arguments.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: OCC said in January 2021 that national banks and federal savings associations may use stablecoins for payment activities, and in March 2025 rescinded its supervisory nonobjection requirement. Innovo's July 2025 article says it had 'already operationalized' stablecoin settlement. Sources: [16], [17], [14].

Evidence note: A report prepared for EPA's Green Power Partnership says REC purchases verify that renewable energy was generated and used, not that new capacity was deployed, and that a unit of voluntary demand cannot generally be mapped to an additional unit of generation on a 1:1 basis. It adds that voluntary demand serves market functions that should affect supply decisions, and it describes tight developer margins. Innovo's article says freed money can go 'elsewhere', without naming a destination. Fortune attributes Glow's construction money to crypto or private equity investors, and Glow says its USDC pool is funded by electricity revenue. Sources: [18], [14], [11], [19].

arguments.title: Encouraging mining adds climate pollution that damages forests and other ecosystems.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Encouraging mining adds climate pollution that damages forests and other ecosystems.

  • Because This argument depends on the bill leading to more Bitcoin mining. See C03. Mining is computer work that earns new Bitcoin and uses a lot of electricity.
  • Because Mining responds to financial rewards with real emissions. At Pennsylvania's Scrubgrass coal plant, which supplies an on-site Bitcoin mine, researchers found that “carbon emissions respond swiftly to mining incentives” [26].
  • Because The risk extends to electricity bought from the grid. The White House report explains that “coal and natural gas often supply electricity generation for each additional unit of electricity demanded in the United States.” [23]
  • Because Buying existing renewable power that other users would consume can shift greenhouse gas (GHG) pollution to those users: “When a crypto-asset mine purchases electricity from existing renewable sources, it displaces the GHG emissions in the near-term, shifting users of renewable sources to fossil fuel sources.” [23]
  • Because Climate damage includes “loss of forests, homes, and infrastructure from increasing wildfires” [23].
  • So The bill encourages an activity whose added power demand worsens climate risks. Protecting forests and ecosystems gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
arguments.con_html:
Response The climate claim skips the step from more stablecoin trading to higher Bitcoin mining rewards.

  • Because The evidence on this step is in C03: trading volume is not price, and studies of Tether found no price effect, with limits.
  • So The trading-volume finding does not establish the price rise that links the bill to the coal plant's added emissions. The grid and renewable-power arguments also start with added mining power demand. They do not establish that S.1582 would cause it.
  • Because Shared response. All the mining arguments share a further response: wider stablecoin use and legal permission may not lead to higher Bitcoin prices or fees for miners. Read it in C03.

Response The climate claim skips the step from more stablecoin trading to higher Bitcoin mining rewards.

  • Because The trading study finds that “stablecoins increase the trading volume of Bitcoin.” [22] Trading volume measures how much changes hands, not how much Bitcoin’s price rises.
  • Because The mining report explains the price link: “As a crypto-asset becomes more valuable, the mining rewards also become more valuable. This attracts more miners and computing resources to solve the cryptographic math problem.” [23]
  • Because A 2018 study’s model separates trading from price gains: “Tether issuances do not impact subsequent Bitcoin returns, however, they do impact traded volumes.” [27] Returns here means price gains or losses.
  • Because A 2020 study of Tether flows to exchanges also reports: “We find no significant effect on the prices of Bitcoin and Ethereum” [28]. The authors add that their aggregate results “do not discount the possibility that price manipulation can occur” [28].

Shared objection The PRO’s claim about wider crypto acceptance overlooks how stablecoin trades reach Bitcoin miners.

  • Because Section 16 authorizes stablecoin business: “Entities regulated by the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators are authorized to engage in the payment stablecoin activities and investments contemplated by this Act” [2]. That permission does not itself establish increased Bitcoin buying.
  • Because Stablecoins also serve people selling Bitcoin. The 2020 study describes investors “liquidating their Bitcoin holdings” [28] into Tether during a price crash.
  • Because Miners receive transaction fees for entries in Bitcoin’s shared record: they collect “fees associated with transactions within the block.” [23]
  • Because Exchange trading is different: “centralized crypto-asset trading platforms typically use off-chain transactions” [23]—trades recorded within the platform rather than in Bitcoin’s shared record.
  • So Trading volume counts activity that includes Bitcoin sales and trades that pay no Bitcoin block fee. It does not measure a rise in Bitcoin prices or fees paid to miners.
  • Because The PRO’s remaining bridge is DeRoche’s forecast: “The more that crypto currency generally is legitimized and used, the more crypto mining there will be” [24].
  • So That broad forecast does not resolve the evidence separating trading growth from price gains or show that the bill would raise miner fees. Legal permission and wider stablecoin use therefore do not establish the extra mining on which all seven reasons depend.

arguments.title: Encouraging mining increases pressure on scarce freshwater.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Encouraging mining increases pressure on scarce freshwater.

  • Because This argument depends on the bill leading to more Bitcoin mining. See C03.
  • Because Mining consumes water through cooling and electricity production. A study explains that “water consumption refers to the portion of water that becomes unavailable for reuse after withdrawal, primarily due to evaporation in cooling systems.” [30] Its measure covers “the freshwater consumed due to both direct and indirect water consumption during the operational stage of Bitcoin mining devices.” [30]
  • Because This demand reaches water-stressed areas. Brookings identifies mining's water risks “especially in drought-prone or resource-scarce areas” [31].
  • So Expanding mining adds demand for a limited natural resource. Protecting scarce freshwater gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose that expansion.
arguments.con_html:
Response Bitcoin's water footprint does not establish that the bill would add freshwater demand.

  • Because For cooling at mining sites, the water study states: “Water usage depends on cooling system types and local climate conditions.” [30]
  • Because For electricity production, it states: “To determine the indirect water footprint, it is important to establish the power demand of the network and the power sources.” [30]
  • So Added water demand requires a change in mining's cooling or power use. Greater trading volume establishes neither. The warning about water scarcity does not show that S.1582 would increase that demand.
  • Because Shared response. All the mining arguments share a further response: wider stablecoin use and legal permission may not lead to higher Bitcoin prices or fees for miners. Read it in C03.

arguments.title: Encouraging mining spreads noise that puts nearby wildlife at risk.
arguments.pro_html:

arguments.title: Required backing protects money that people with little financial cushion need for essentials.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Required backing protects money that people with little financial cushion need for essentials.

  • Because Issuers licensed under the bill must keep reserves worth at least the full amount they owe users. See C04.
  • Because Reuse is limited to listed reserve-investment, custody, and cash-out needs. Outside those purposes, reserves “may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, either directly or indirectly” [3]. To rehypothecate means to reuse an asset as security for a loan.
  • Because Safe, readily available backing supports repayment: “they need to be backed by safe and liquid assets, like cash, Treasury bills, and central bank reserves, so they can offer convertibility at par.” [5] At par means at the full promised value.
  • Because Ordinary crypto users are less able to absorb losses: “most retail participants lack the resources, information, and financial resilience needed to navigate this volatile space.” [6]
  • Because Dollar-linked coins also serve people facing unstable currencies: “Stablecoins can also mitigate local currency and inflationary risks, major advantages in volatile markets.” [7]
  • Because Aid recipients already use them. UNHCR “successfully executed a small pilot to distribute cash assistance to a group of people displaced by the war in Ukraine in Circle Internet Financial’s USD Coin (USDC)” [8].
  • So Enforceable backing rules protect against coins issued without enough money to repay users. That protects small savings and aid payments, including money vulnerable people abroad need for food, shelter, and care.

arguments.title: Cash-out rules and advance fee notices protect people who depend on ready access to their money.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Cash-out rules and advance fee notices protect people who depend on ready access to their money.

  • Because Issuers must publish procedures for “timely redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins” [3]. Redemption means exchanging a coin for money. Discretionary limits require a regulator's decision: “any discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be imposed by a State qualified payment stablecoin regulator, the Corporation, the Comptroller, or the Board” [3].
  • Because Purchase and cash-out fees must be disclosed in plain language, and “such fees can only be changed upon not less than 7 days' prior notice to consumers” [3].
  • So Issuers lose the freedom to impose their own discretionary cash-out limits or change fees without warning. This protects people whose essential spending leaves little room for delays or surprise charges.
arguments.con_html:
Response The PRO leaves out the link between issuer cash-out terms and the terms for spending money held through other firms.

  • Because Section 4 regulates “the issuer's redemption policy” [3]. The 7-day notice is the issuer's duty.
  • Because Circle's pre-vote prospectus explains: “Transactions between third parties may be subject to fees charged by the parties to the transaction or the secondary marketplace on which the transaction occurs.” [9] Those fees and terms “are governed by agreements between the parties to the transactions and/or the rules of the secondary marketplace” [9]. The secondary market is where people trade coins with each other, not with the issuer.
  • So This response does not dispute the protection for people who redeem directly with an issuer. It challenges the wider step: the issuer's notice does not govern every wallet, exchange, or cash-pickup firm's charges and delays, and the PRO has not shown how the change improves access for households relying on those firms.

arguments.title: Checked reports and truthful marketing protect people who cannot investigate a financial firm themselves.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Checked reports and truthful marketing protect people who cannot investigate a financial firm themselves.

  • Because Issuers must “publish the monthly composition of the issuer's reserves on the website of the issuer” [3]. This means listing what the reserves are made of. Monthly reports must be “examined by a registered public accounting firm.” [3]
  • Because Senior executives must submit “a certification as to the accuracy of the monthly report” [3]. This makes named managers answer for the information users receive.
  • Because The bill bans false claims of government backing or insurance: “It shall be unlawful to represent that payment stablecoins are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, guaranteed by the United States Government, or subject to Federal deposit insurance or Federal share insurance.” [3]
  • Because Such deception harms people relying on savings. Brookings describes Celsius customers misled about safety or insurance: “Many victims had invested their retirement savings or emergency funds.” [6]
  • So Public reports, outside checks, and marketing rules make accurate safety information less dependent on a customer's expertise or wealth. That gives people [NAME] does not know fairer treatment when deciding whom to trust with their money.
arguments.con_html:
Response The PRO's Celsius example does not show the added protection it is used to illustrate.

  • Because The cited harm concerns “major crypto platforms such as Celsius and Voyager” [6]. A report about a coin issuer's reserves is not a report about a separate platform's ability to return its customers' money.
  • Because The FDIC stated in 2022: “The Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDI Act) prohibits any person from representing or implying that an uninsured product is FDIC–insured or from knowingly misrepresenting the extent and manner of deposit insurance.” [12] So the deposit-insurance part of the bill's marketing ban overlaps an existing prohibition.
  • So This leaves the bill's reserve reports, executive certifications, and ban on claims of U.S. government backing unanswered. The Celsius example does not establish how those provisions relieve customers of judging the safety of a separate platform holding their savings.

arguments.title: Customer ownership and repayment priority protect users when a firm fails.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Customer ownership and repayment priority protect users when a firm fails.

  • Because Firms holding stablecoin assets for customers must treat them as the customer's property and generally keep them separate. See C07.
  • Because Customers' claims to coins held by those firms rank ahead of other creditors, unless the customer expressly agrees otherwise: “the claims of the customer against such person with respect to such payment stablecoins shall have priority” [3].
  • Because If an issuer fails, holders have first claim to required reserves, shared in proportion to their claims. See C05.
  • Because If required reserves are missing, unpaid coin claims also come first against the issuer's remaining assets, up to the missing amount. See C06.
  • Because In a court case to reorganize an issuer, a regulator “shall raise, and shall appear and be heard on, any issue, including the protection of customers” [3].
  • So Users gain protection against unrelated business debts, a proportionate share of reserves, and a public voice in the issuer's failure. These rules support just treatment of customers who lack the power to bargain for protection themselves.
arguments.con_html:
Response The PRO's failure protection does not reach Treasury backing that a lender can take first.

Treasury backing a lender can take first. Section 4 permits using Treasury reserves as collateral for borrowing to meet redemptions: “creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins” [UNC 3]. Brookings explains these secured loans, called repurchase agreements or repo: in bankruptcy, “the repo lender could seize the Treasury collateral if the stablecoin issuer could not return the cash.” [UNC 13] Then “assets in segregated accounts would fall short of what is needed for 1:1 redemption.” [UNC 13] A right to share those assets does not restore the seized collateral.

  • So This leaves the protection against other business debts unanswered. It challenges the PRO's description of holders' claim to a full proportionate share of reserves where backing has been pledged in this way.

arguments.title: Screening managers and public enforcement protect customers from misconduct.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 Screening managers and public enforcement protect customers from misconduct.

  • Because The bill excludes managers convicted of specified crimes: “The bill would prohibit anyone who has been convicted of certain financial crimes of being an officer or director of an issuer.” [4]
  • Because Federal licensing reviews must assess “The competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders of the applicant” [3].
  • Because Federal regulators can order a violating issuer to “take affirmative action to correct the conditions resulting from any such violation or practice.” [3] State regulators receive “supervisory, examination, and enforcement authority over all State qualified payment stablecoin issuers of such State.” [3]
  • So Public officials must check managers and gain powers to correct misconduct. Customers receive protection that does not depend on their own money or skill in investigating and challenging a firm.
arguments.con_html:
Response The PRO's statement that public officials must check managers leaves out the bill's approval route without a completed decision.

  • Because Section 5 sets the decision deadline at “Not later than 120 days after receiving a substantially complete application under subsection (a)” [3]. If the regulator misses the deadline, “the application shall be deemed approved.” [3] Deemed approved means treated as approved even without a decision.

arguments.title: Required controls on criminal funds protect victims and help preserve stolen money for recovery.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 8 Required controls on criminal funds protect victims and help preserve stolen money for recovery.

  • Because Tether's coins appear in criminal cases. A Bloomberg opinion piece says: “Its USDT coins have been seized and forfeited in cases involving fraud, terrorist financing, sanctions violations and other criminal activity.” [16] It adds: “(The company denies wrongdoing.)” [16]
  • Because Section 4 requires suspicious-transaction reporting. See C27. It also requires the ability to block, freeze and reject impermissible transactions. See C13. Section 5 requires compliance programs aimed in particular at “cartels and organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations” [3].
  • Because Section 8 conditions U.S. trading of foreign coins on the issuer being able to comply and complying with lawful orders. See C14.
  • Because Freezing and seizing proceeds serves victims. In a crypto-fraud case, the U.S. Secret Service described work to “identify victims and seize these funds so that they can eventually be returned to their rightful owners.” [17]
  • So Requiring issuers to detect and block criminal transfers makes it harder to move stolen funds beyond recovery or use them to finance further harm. This serves justice for victims across borders, including people [NAME] will never meet.
arguments.con_html:
Response The PRO's inference about detecting criminal transfers leaves out a monitoring limit on issuer duties. Identifying criminal transfers is a separate task from freezing funds once identified.

  • Because The CRS warning and FinCEN's April 2026 proposal are in C18. FinCEN's text is a proposal, open to comment. It is not the bill.
  • So This leaves the freezing capability and the condition on foreign issuers unanswered. It challenges the PRO's inference that duties placed on issuers will detect criminal transfers that move away from their direct customers.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: FinCEN clarified in 2013 that AML/CFT reporting requirements apply to crypto transmission. DOJ's cited recovery case was announced on June 18, 2025, and thanks Tether for its proactive assistance. Sources: [20], [17].

Evidence note: FinCEN and OFAC's April 2026 proposed rule would apply secondary-market obligations to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. It does not propose requiring issuers, as part of an AML/CFT program, to monitor secondary-market activity or file SARs on secondary-market transactions, and it requests comment. Section 9(d) rulemaking is separate. Sources: [19].

arguments.title: Limits on commercial use of payment data give customers a say over firms' use of their private financial lives.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 10 Limits on commercial use of payment data give customers a say over firms' use of their private financial lives.

  • Because For public companies mainly engaged outside finance, approval to issue coins requires limits on using customers' private transaction data without their consent. See C20.
  • So Requiring permission stops these firms from taking those commercial benefits from private payment histories without customers' agreement. Giving customers a say in that bargain supports just treatment.
arguments.con_html:
Response Requiring permission does not by itself establish the just treatment the PRO infers from a customer's agreement.

  • Because The paragraph sets no requirement that the service remain available when the consumer refuses those uses.
  • Because The separate ban on forced purchases concerns “an additional paid product or service” [3]. Agreement to data use is not an additional paid product.
  • So This provision alone does not rule out making agreement a condition of service. The PRO needs a reason why obtaining that agreement gives customers fair control over their private payment histories. The word consent does not supply it.

arguments.title: A nationwide licensing route widens opportunity for new providers and the people they serve.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 11 A nationwide licensing route widens opportunity for new providers and the people they serve.

  • Because Repeated state licensing creates a barrier for nonbank payment firms: “the time and cost of obtaining such licenses can be daunting for Fintechs” [23].
  • Because Section 5 replaces extra state licensing for federally approved issuers. Its provisions “supersede and preempt any State requirement for a charter, license, or other authorization to do business” [3] for those issuers. To preempt means federal law takes the place of state law.
  • Because Both banks and nonbanks can apply: “Stablecoins could be issued by banks and credit unions (through subsidiaries) or nonbanks.” [4] Public networks remain eligible: “The issuance of a payment stablecoin on an open, public, or decentralized network shall not be a valid ground for denial of an application received under subsection (a).” [3]
  • Because This matters for access: “Stablecoins enable users to save in a stable currency and transact globally without a bank account” [24].
  • Because Stablecoins already offer useful transfer options: “Where permitted, stablecoins offer a faster and cheaper alternative to traditional remittance solutions. This is especially important for migrant workers and in solving perennial small business challenges.” [25] Remittances are money sent home to family.
  • Because The stakes reach vulnerable households. The Dallas Fed describes money sent home to Mexico: “These remittances are a valuable lifeline for millions of households in Mexico, especially in the poorest states.” [26]
  • Because Smaller firms also face barriers that these services address: stablecoins can “widen access to trade and finance for smaller companies that struggle with correspondent banking.” [24] Correspondent banking means banks using other banks to handle international payments.
  • So Removing repeated licensing gives new providers a fairer chance to offer these services nationwide under the bill's safeguards. This lowers a barrier to serving people who need bankless payments or lower-cost international transfers, including migrant families and small firms. That advances equal financial opportunity beyond established banks and their customers.

arguments.title: Clear approval criteria and appeals require fair treatment of new applicants.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 12 Clear approval criteria and appeals require fair treatment of new applicants.

  • Because Federal regulators may deny a complete application only on safety grounds: “the activities of the applicant would be unsafe or unsound based on the factors described in subsection (c).” [3]
  • Because A denial must identify shortcomings and offer “actionable recommendations on how the applicant could address the identified material shortcomings.” [3]
  • Because Applicants can request a hearing to challenge rejection: “Regulators would have to justify denials and permit applicants to appeal.” [4]
  • So People seeking to start a qualified provider gain stated criteria, reasons for rejection, and a way to challenge mistakes. This supports [NAME]'s concern for just treatment by public officials.
arguments.con_html:
Response Procedures for a new federal approval power do not establish fairer treatment than the law they replace.

  • Because The bill makes U.S. issuance by someone without its permission unlawful: “It shall be unlawful for any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States.” [3] Its internal appeal reviews decisions under that new permission requirement.
  • So The stated criteria, reasons and appeal rules constrain a licensing power the bill itself creates. The PRO has not established that applicants receive less arbitrary treatment than under the law in force on July 17, 2025.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: Federal law already required a brief statement of grounds for agency denials, with exceptions, and judicial review for legal wrongs from agency action; New York's route had public standards. Sources: [27], [28], [11].

arguments.title: The ban on issuer-paid interest blocks one incentive to pull deposits away from community lending.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 13 The ban on issuer-paid interest blocks one incentive to pull deposits away from community lending.

  • Because Section 4 bars issuers from paying holders interest or other returns just for holding or using a coin. Such interest could otherwise draw money from bank deposits that fund loans. See C12.
  • Because Deposit losses threaten credit in places with few lending options: “This impact will be especially acute in rural and low-income areas” [29].
  • So The ban prevents issuers from using direct interest payments to draw those deposits. Blocking that incentive protects a source of loans for households and small firms in communities where limited credit already restricts opportunity.
arguments.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: The PPI lending warning builds on a $6.6 trillion figure that CRS and the Treasury advisory presentation describe as at risk or hypothetical. CEA's April 2026 baseline estimates that eliminating stablecoin yield would raise bank lending by $2.1 billion (0.02%), with $500 million from community banks (0.026%). Sources: [30], [31], [32].

Evidence note: CRS reports that much retail stablecoin use occurs through exchanges, that GENIUS does not explicitly prevent exchanges from paying rewards on coins they hold, that many do, and that Circle pays part of its reserve interest to Coinbase. CRS also says the issuer is prohibited from paying interest in a direct issuer-to-customer model, that the restriction would presumably apply to self-custody, and that 'holder' is undefined. Coinbase attributes part of its USDC balance growth to its rewards program. AAF says issuers can effectively circumvent the ban through exchanges or third parties. Sources: [30], [33], [34].

arguments.title: Moving household money into stablecoins exposes essential savings to uninsured losses.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Moving household money into stablecoins exposes essential savings to uninsured losses.

  • Because This argument needs some household money to move into stablecoins. See C02.
  • Because Replacing an insured bank balance with tokens removes the insurance on that money: stablecoins are “not federally insured” [4].
  • Because The backing can itself lose value: “the permissible reserve assets include uninsured deposits in banks and shares of credit unions” [13]; “uninsured deposits are risky and illiquid” [13]. The source's sentence continues: “raising the possibility that stablecoins backed by these assets will not offer a stable value and will be prone to runs” [13], unless those risks are reduced by “capital, liquidity, and risk management standards” [13].
  • Because The bill also permits borrowing against Treasury securities held as backing. If the issuer cannot repay that loan, the lender can take those securities first: “assets in segregated accounts would fall short of what is needed for 1:1 redemption.” [13]. Segregated accounts hold assets kept apart for coin holders.

arguments.title: The bill expands payments without establishing the refund rights and help users need after theft or mistakes.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill expands payments without establishing the refund rights and help users need after theft or mistakes.

  • Because This argument needs more people to use these coins for payments. See C02.
  • Because Established card laws protect against unauthorized transfers: “The Truth-In-Lending Act and the EFTA provide important protection when there are unauthorized transfers.” [39]. EFTA is the federal law governing debit cards and other electronic payments.
  • Because The stablecoin law adds “no protection for unauthorized transfers” [39]. It also has no required process for handling errors. See C25.
  • Because It also omits tools for spotting and resolving missing payments: “Periodic Account Statement Not Required” [39]; “No Customer Service Requirements” [39].
  • Because Users cannot sue just for a breach of the new law's consumer rules: it “does not grant consumers a private right of action” [39].
  • So People who cannot replace stolen or missing payment money need clear refund duties and a way to enforce them. Expanding stablecoin payments without establishing those rights gives [NAME] a reason to protect the people least able to absorb the loss.
arguments.con_html:
Response Listing protections absent from this bill does not establish that the payment arrangements it would expand lack enforceable rights under other laws.

  • Because Section 6(c) preserves existing rights: “Nothing in this Act may be construed to modify or otherwise affect any right or remedy under any Federal consumer financial law” [3].
  • Because Before July 2025, a federal district court had applied the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to personal cryptocurrency accounts. It held: “Its terms, when properly construed, cover the electronic transfer of funds such as cryptocurrency.” [40]
  • Because The PRO's consumer-law source also recognizes claims under other consumer statutes: “These laws do not preclude consumers from suing in court.” [39] It adds that the bill's preemption section “may preclude consumers from successfully asserting a violation of state law.” [39]
  • So The absence of a new right to sue under S.1582 does not erase payment-law or contract claims, though their reach is unsettled. The PRO needs to establish the claimed refund and help gap under the laws governing the accounts in question. Omissions from this one statute do not establish it.

arguments.title: The bill removes an existing fraud watchdog from permitted stablecoin sales.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill removes an existing fraud watchdog from permitted stablecoin sales.

  • Because The U.S. commodity regulator (the CFTC) has used its fraud powers against false stablecoin reserve claims. Its Tether order required “a civil monetary penalty of $41 million” [41] for “making untrue or misleading statements and omissions of material fact” [41].
  • Because Section 17 removes permitted tokens from that regulator's commodity-fraud law: “The term `commodity' does not include a payment stablecoin issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [3]. A permitted issuer is one approved under the bill.
  • So Removing this route for pursuing dishonest sales takes away a protection already used for stablecoin customers. [NAME]'s concern for protecting weaker customers from powerful firms gives a reason to oppose that loss.
arguments.con_html:
Response A change of regulator does not establish a loss of protection against the reserve fraud in the Tether example.

  • Because The case concerned claims about backing and outside checks: “Tether misrepresented to customers and the market that Tether maintained sufficient U.S. dollar reserves” [41]; “Tether falsely represented that it would undergo routine, professional audits” [41].
  • Because Section 4 makes full backing a legal duty, “on an at least 1 to 1 basis” [3]. It requires monthly reserve information to be “examined by a registered public accounting firm” [3] and punishes an executive's certification made “knowing that such certification is false” [3].
  • Because Section 6 lets federal supervisors order an issuer to “take affirmative action to correct the conditions resulting from any such violation or practice.” [3] Section 7 gives state supervisors “supervisory, examination, and enforcement authority” [3] over their approved issuers.
  • So The cited misconduct remains subject to direct backing, reporting, and enforcement duties. Counting the lost commodity-law route without assessing these replacements does not show that customers lose protection against that fraud.

arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Nationwide approval can take effect without a completed safety decision or another state's licensing check.

  • Because A substantially complete federal application must be decided within 120 days. If the regulator misses the deadline, “the application shall be deemed approved.” [3]. This means it is treated as approved even without a decision.

  • So Such an issuer can gain nationwide access through official silence, while states lose the power to require another license before it serves their residents. Protecting residents from entry without a completed safety decision gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this rule.
